text: Patent prosecution is the process of interacting with the Patent Office to obtain a granted patent. It begins after filing and continues until the patent is either granted or abandoned. Key stages include: publication (18 months from priority), request for examination (RFE within 48 months), examination by Controller, First Examination Report (FER), applicant's response to objections, hearing if needed, and grant/refusal decision. For AYUSH patents, prosecution often involves defending against Section 3(d) (new form of known substance) and Section 3(p) (traditional knowledge) objections.

The First Examination Report (FER) is the Controller's initial assessment of the patent application. FER typically raises objections on: formal defects (missing documents, fee shortfalls), novelty (prior art citations), inventive step (obviousness), industrial applicability, Section 3 exclusions (for AYUSH: Section 3(d) and 3(p) are common), claim clarity and support. Applicant must respond within 6 months (extendable by 3 months on request). Response should address EACH objection point with arguments and/or claim amendments. Failure to respond leads to deemed abandonment.

Effective FER response strategy: 1) Carefully read each objection — understand what Controller is asking. 2) For novelty objections — distinguish claims from cited prior art, highlight differences, narrow claims if needed. 3) For obviousness — argue unexpected results, synergistic effects, technical prejudice overcome. 4) For Section 3(d) — provide comparative data showing enhanced efficacy (30% improvement guideline from Novartis case). 5) For Section 3(p) — provide evidence of novelty over traditional knowledge, TKDL search report. 6) Submit affidavits/declarations with supporting data. 7) Propose claim amendments in proper format. 8) Request hearing if complex issues require oral arguments.

Claim amendments during prosecution must follow Rule 81: amendments cannot broaden the scope of claims beyond the originally filed specification. Types: 1) Narrowing claims — adding limitations from dependent claims or specification. 2) Clarifying claims — fixing ambiguity without changing scope. 3) Deleting claims — removing rejected claims to proceed with allowed ones. 4) Adding new claims — only if supported by original specification. For AYUSH patents: common amendments include adding dosage ranges, specific formulation parameters, or clinical efficacy data to overcome Section 3(d) objections.

A divisional application can be filed when the original application claims more than one invention (lack of unity of invention). Under Section 16, the applicant can voluntarily divide, or the Controller may require division. Divisional retains the parent's filing/priority date for the divided-out claims. Key rules: 1) File before grant of parent. 2) Claims must be different from parent (no overlap). 3) Each divisional is examined independently. 4) Useful for AYUSH when one application covers both formulation and process — can divide to pursue both. Filing fee same as new application; prosecution separate.

Hearing before the Controller occurs when: 1) Applicant requests oral hearing to argue against FER objections. 2) Pre-grant opposition is filed. 3) Controller needs clarification. Procedure: Submit hearing request in writing, pay fee (Rs 15,000 for e-filing), hearing scheduled (typically 1-3 months later), prepare written submissions in advance, present oral arguments at hearing, Controller issues order within 1-3 months. For AYUSH patents facing Section 3(d)/3(p) objections, hearings are often crucial to explain scientific data and distinguish from prior art.

Expedited examination available for: 1) Startups (DPIIT recognized) — additional fee Rs 60,000 (e-filing). 2) Female applicants — same fee. 3) Small entities. 4) Government institutions. 5) Applicants who chose India as ISA/IPEA under PCT. Timeline: examination report within 120 days of request (vs normal 1-3 years). To request: file Form 18A after RFE, pay expedited fee, submit all pending documents. For AYUSH startups, this significantly accelerates the process — can get to grant in 12-18 months vs 3-5 years normal.

India does NOT have continuation or continuation-in-part (CIP) applications like the US. Once an application is filed, you cannot add new matter. Options available: 1) Convention application — file new application claiming priority from foreign filing (within 12 months). 2) Divisional application — divide claims from pending parent. 3) New application — file fresh without priority claim. For AYUSH R&D generating incremental innovations, file new applications for each improvement rather than trying to add to pending applications.

After all objections are addressed and Controller is satisfied, the patent is granted. Grant process: 1) Controller issues 'Intention to Grant' communication. 2) Applicant pays balance fee if any. 3) Grant order issued. 4) Patent published in Patent Office Journal (Part I — specifications, Part II — grant). 5) Certificate of Grant issued with patent number and grant date. 6) Patent term: 20 years from filing date (not grant date). 7) First renewal due 2 years from filing date (even if still in prosecution). For AYUSH patents, average time to grant: 3-5 years (faster with expedited examination).

If a patent application lapses due to missed deadline (e.g., failure to respond to FER within time), restoration is possible under Rule 137: 1) File petition for restoration within 18 months of abandonment. 2) Show 'unintentional' lapse — provide reasons. 3) Pay restoration fee (Rs 2,400 e-filing for natural person). 4) Submit the missed response/document. 5) Controller decides on merits. Success rate depends on reasons — genuine oversight typically restored; deliberate abandonment rarely. For AYUSH applicants: calendar ALL deadlines, but know restoration is a safety net.

Indian Patent Office has 4 branches with territorial jurisdiction: 1) Delhi (Head Office) — applications from Delhi, Haryana, HP, J&K, Ladakh, Punjab, Rajasthan, UP, Uttarakhand, Chandigarh. 2) Mumbai — Maharashtra, Gujarat, Goa, MP, Chhattisgarh, Daman, Dadra. 3) Chennai — AP, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Lakshadweep, Andaman. 4) Kolkata — WB, Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, Assam, NE states, Sikkim. Jurisdiction based on applicant's address (first applicant if multiple). e-Filing works regardless of jurisdiction.

Section 146 requires patent holders to file a Statement of Working (Form 27) annually, disclosing whether and how the patent is being worked in India. Due: within 3 months of every financial year (by June 30). Information required: whether patent is being worked, extent of working (quantity, value), reasons if not working, license details if any. Penalty for non-filing: up to Rs 10 lakh. For AYUSH patent holders: maintain records of production, sales, and licensing to accurately report. Non-working for 3+ years may trigger compulsory licensing.

Unlike some countries, India does NOT provide patent term extension (PTE) for regulatory delays. Patent term is fixed at 20 years from filing date regardless of prosecution time or drug approval delays. This affects AYUSH products requiring CDSCO/AYUSH Ministry approvals — no compensation for years lost in clinical trials or regulatory review. Strategy: file patent early in development, pursue expedited examination, fast-track regulatory approvals. Some suggest term extension for pharma/AYUSH should be introduced; currently not available.

Abandoned application: deemed abandoned due to failure to respond to official actions within time, or non-payment of fees. Can be restored within 18 months if 'unintentional'. Withdrawn application: applicant voluntarily requests withdrawal (Form 29). No restoration possible once withdrawn. Strategic withdrawal: if application is weak (prior art found), withdraw before publication to prevent it becoming prior art against future applications. For AYUSH: if initial formulation doesn't work, withdraw and file fresh with improved version rather than amending.

Double patenting is not explicitly prohibited in Indian law, but the Patent Office may reject claims that are substantially identical to claims in another granted patent or pending application by the same applicant. Types: 1) Same invention double patenting — identical claims (clearly rejected). 2) Obviousness-type double patenting — claims obvious variant of own earlier patent (may be rejected). For AYUSH portfolio: ensure each application has distinct claims. If dividing or filing related applications, make claims clearly different. Terminal disclaimer (US concept) not available in India.
